package.name: Process
package.description: The running process: its command-line arguments, environment, identifier and exit

modules.name: Arguments
modules.header:
The command-line arguments the process was started with.
Each argument is native text: bytes on the Unix systems and UTF-16 code units on Windows, exactly as the system
handed them over. Nothing obliges an argument to be valid UTF-8 or valid UTF-16, so it is a view of native units
rather than `String`, and `ToText` is the fallible step to text. The first argument is the program as it was
invoked, which is a name or a path the caller chose rather than a reliable way to find the executable.
Every view borrows storage the process owns for its whole life, so arguments may be kept and passed anywhere without
copying.

modules.name: Buffer
modules.header:
A growable run of plain values, owned through an allocator: the units of a command line, the bytes a child wrote.
Only plain values — units, bytes, addresses — go in one, so growing it copies bytes and destroying it only gives
the storage back.

modules.name: Capture
modules.header:
Running a program to completion and keeping everything it wrote.
A child blocks once a pipe it writes to is full, so reading its output to the end and only then its error would
leave a child that fills its error pipe first waiting forever. The error is therefore read on a second thread while
this one reads the output, and both finish when the child closes its ends.

modules.name: Child
modules.header:
A started child process, how it finished, and the pipes to its standard streams.
The pipes are ordinary streams: a `PipeWriter` is an `Io::Writer` into the child's standard input, and a `PipeReader`
an `Io::Reader` from its standard output or error. Each owns its end of the pipe and closes it when dropped, which
is how a child reading its input learns that no more will come.

modules.name: Command
modules.header:
Describing a program to start — its arguments, directory, environment and standard streams — and starting it.
A command collects its parts as native text as they are given. A part the system could not take, such as text with
a NUL in it, is remembered as the command's first failure and reported when it is started, so the parts can be
given one after another without checking each.
On Linux, FreeBSD and macOS the child is started with the C library's `posix_spawnp`, which finds the program
through `PATH`, sets up its streams and directory, and reports a program that could not be started as an error
rather than as a child that exits. On Windows it is started with `CreateProcessW`, from a command line quoted the way
the C runtime splits one, so each argument arrives as it was given.

modules.name: Environment
modules.header:
The process's environment: `name=value` pairs, as the system started the process with them and as changed since.
Names and values are native text, so they are views of native units rather than `String`. A name is matched exactly
on the Unix systems and without regard to ASCII case on Windows, which is each system's own rule.
Changes made through `SetVariable` and `RemoveVariable` are kept in a table beside the environment the process
started with, and every reader here consults the table first, so `Variable`, `Environment` and every process this
package starts see them. Their text is never freed, which is what keeps every view this package has handed out
valid for the life of the process; an environment is changed rarely enough that this costs little. Windows is also
told of each change, so code that asks the system sees it too; the C library's own environment on the Unix systems
is not changed.

modules.name: Executable
modules.header:
The file the process is running.
`Argument(0)` is whatever the parent passed as the program's name, which may be a bare name found on the search
path, a relative path, or anything at all; it is no way to find the executable again. Each system knows the file it
loaded and says so: Windows through `GetModuleFileNameW`, Linux through the `/proc/self/exe` link, FreeBSD through
the `kern.proc.pathname` sysctl and macOS through `_NSGetExecutablePath`. The answer is asked for each time, into a
buffer grown until the whole path fits.

modules.name: Exit
modules.header:
What a process can say about itself: who it is, and that it is done.
`Exit` ends the process at once with a status for its parent. Nothing is flushed, unwound or destroyed on the way:
a buffered writer that has not been flushed loses what it holds, which is why returning from `Main` is the ordinary
way to finish and `Exit` is for leaving from somewhere `Main` cannot be returned to.

modules.name: Failure
modules.header:
What a failed system call means, as an `IoError`, and text turned into native units for a command line.
The raw code rides along in every error, so a caller who needs the system's own reason still has it.

modules.name: Native
modules.header:
Where each system keeps the arguments and environment a process was started with, read once and kept.
Linux and FreeBSD leave them on the stack the kernel built: the argument count, the argument pointers and a null,
then the environment pointers and a null. The entry stub keeps that address, and `Core::ProcessStartFrame` hands it
over. macOS has dyld record the same vectors and publishes them through libSystem. Windows hands over one command
line and one environment block instead; the command line is split once, the way the C runtime splits it, and both
results are kept for the life of the process, so every view this package gives out stays valid as long as the
process does.
Nothing here is written after the first read, and the first read happens before any caller could share the results,
so a program with one thread needs nothing more. A program that starts threads should read its arguments before it
does.

doc.summary: The value of the environment variable `name`, or none when it is not set.
doc.markdown:
The value of the environment variable `name`, or none when it is not set.
`name` is UTF-8 text. It is matched exactly on the Unix systems and without regard to ASCII case on Windows, which
is how each system matches names. A variable set or removed with `SetVariable` or `RemoveVariable` reads as it was
last changed. When the starting environment names a variable twice, the first is the one returned, as the C
library's `getenv` returns it. A variable set to the empty string is present, with an empty value. The view borrows
storage the process owns for its whole life. Runs in time linear in the size of the environment and allocates
nothing.

doc.returns: the variable's value, or none when no variable has that name

items.signature: pub func CurrentExecutable(allocator: Allocator) -> PathBuffer ! IoError

doc.summary: The path of the executable file the process is running, as the system loaded it.
doc.markdown:
The path of the executable file the process is running, as the system loaded it.
Unlike `Argument(0)`, which is whatever the parent chose to pass, this is the file itself, so a program that runs
itself again or finds files installed beside it can rely on it. Windows, Linux and FreeBSD give an absolute path
with symbolic links resolved; macOS gives the path the executable was loaded by, which may be relative to the
directory the process started in or pass through links. Fails with `NotFound` when the system cannot say, as when
Linux has no `/proc` mounted, and with `LimitExceeded` when the path cannot be stored.

params.name: allocator
params.markdown: what the path is kept in

doc.returns: the executable's path

doc.summary: Ends the whole process at once, reporting `code` to its parent.
doc.markdown:
Ends the whole process at once, reporting `code` to its parent.
Every thread stops. Nothing is flushed, unwound or destroyed: the system reclaims memory and descriptors, and data
still buffered in the process is lost, so flush what must be written first. On the Unix systems the parent sees
only the low eight bits of `code`; on Windows it sees all thirty-two. Does not return.

params.name: code
params.markdown: the status to report, zero for success by convention

doc.summary: The identifier the system gave this process.
doc.markdown:
The identifier the system gave this process.
Stable for the life of the process and unique among running processes, but reused once the process has exited.
Cannot fail and allocates nothing.
doc.returns: the process identifier
